reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant skeletal muscle channelopathy with reduced penetrance, especially in females, so the family history may appear incomplete.
Most cases are caused by mutations in CACNA1S (Cav1.1), with a minority due to SCN4A (Nav1.4), both affecting voltage-sensor domains.
Episodes of flaccid weakness occur with a low serum potassium, the reverse of the hyperkalaemic form.
Attacks are commonly nocturnal or on waking and last longer than in the hyperkalaemic form, sometimes for many hours to over a day.
Typical triggers are carbohydrate-rich meals, rest after strenuous exercise, cold, stress and alcohol.
Myotonia is absent, which helps separate it from the hyperkalaemic form and paramyotonia congenita.
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is an important acquired mimic, particularly in men of Asian ancestry with hyperthyroidism.
Respiratory and bulbar muscles are usually spared, though severe attacks can rarely threaten ventilation.
reference.pathophysiology: Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is caused by missense mutations in the voltage-sensing domains of the skeletal muscle calcium channel Cav1.1 (CACNA1S) or, less often, the sodium channel Nav1.4 (SCN4A). These mutations create an aberrant gating-pore (omega) current, an abnormal leak of cations through the voltage sensor that is normally sealed. In the setting of a low extracellular potassium, this leak produces paradoxical depolarisation of the sarcolemma rather than the expected hyperpolarisation, driving sodium channels into inactivation and leaving the membrane inexcitable, so that the fibre cannot generate action potentials and becomes paralysed. Because low extracellular potassium favours this depolarised, inexcitable state, shifts of potassium into cells triggered by carbohydrate or exercise recovery precipitate attacks.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary hypokalaemia (renal tubular acidosis, Gitelman or Bartter syndrome, diuretics, hyperaldosteronism)
additionalInvestigations: Serum potassium measured during an attack
Electrocardiogram looking for hypokalaemic changes such as U waves
Thyroid function tests to exclude thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
Genetic testing of CACNA1S and SCN4A
Electromyography with the long exercise test
Renal function, acid-base status and urinary potassium to exclude secondary causes
redFlags: Respiratory muscle involvement during a severe attack
Undiagnosed thyrotoxicosis as the underlying cause
Features pointing to a secondary cause of potassium loss
reference.prognosis: Acute attacks tend to diminish in frequency with age and overall life expectancy is normal, but many patients develop a chronic progressive vacuolar myopathy with fixed proximal weakness in later life. Trigger avoidance and prophylactic therapy reduce attack burden.
pitfalls: Over-replacing potassium and provoking rebound hyperkalaemia.
Missing thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, which is treated by controlling the hyperthyroidism.
Being misled by apparently absent family history because of reduced penetrance, particularly in women.
Failing to distinguish primary disease from secondary hypokalaemia due to renal or gastrointestinal losses.
Assuming a carbohydrate load or glucose-insulin is safe when it can precipitate an attack.
references: International consensus on the diagnosis and management of the primary periodic paralyses
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat acute attacks with oral potassium supplementation, monitoring for rebound hyperkalaemia and reserving cautious intravenous replacement for severe or respiratory involvement
Prevent attacks by avoiding recognised triggers such as carbohydrate-rich meals, rest after strenuous exercise, cold and alcohol
Use carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as dichlorphenamide or acetazolamide as prophylaxis to reduce attack frequency
Add a potassium-sparing diuretic and advise a low-carbohydrate, low-sodium diet where attacks persist
Monitor for the chronic progressive vacuolar myopathy that can develop with age and support fixed weakness with physiotherapy
Ensure careful anaesthetic planning, warning against depolarising muscle relaxants and glucose-rich fluids that can provoke attacks
Exclude and treat thyrotoxic and secondary causes before committing to lifelong prophylaxis
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant channelopathy, noting reduced penetrance
